title: Find Disconnected Network Regions (DFS)
real_world_story: After a fiber cut or a failure at a switching center, the company must quickly find out whether the network has broken into separate parts. A depth-first exploration from every unvisited device reveals exactly how many isolated regions the network currently has.

real_world_connection.input_represents: Devices and the links that connect them
real_world_connection.output_represents: The number of separate connected regions in the network
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Exploring one region completely before starting the next

problem_statement: Given N devices numbered 0 to N-1 and E undirected communication links, determine how many separate connected regions the network contains using Depth-First Search. A region is a maximal set of devices that can all reach one another through links.
task: Return the number of connected regions in the network.
input_format: The first line contains two integers N and E. The next E lines each contain two integers u v describing an undirected communication link between devices u and v.
output_format: Print the number of connected regions in the network.

examples.explanation: Devices 0, 1 and 2 form one region, devices 3 and 4 form a second region, and device 5 is isolated, so there are 3 regions.

expected_algorithm.name: Graph DFS
expected_algorithm.reason: Starting a DFS from every unvisited device visits exactly one connected region at a time, so counting how many times a new DFS is started gives the number of network regions.

hint: Start a fresh DFS from every device that has not been visited yet.
Each new DFS start means one more connected region.
Use an explicit stack, or raise the recursion limit, because the network can contain up to 100000 devices.
real_world_takeaway: Counting connected regions with DFS tells a communication company how badly the network is fragmented after a failure and which groups of devices need separate attention.
